slots.practicalActivity: Take a normalized OLTP order system (Customers, Orders, OrderLines, Products in 3NF) and sketch, by hand, what a dimensional (OLAP-style) version of the same data would look like. Label which OLTP tables would collapse into a single dimension and which would feed a fact table.
slots.deliverable: A hand-drawn before/after sketch: the 3NF OLTP tables on one side, the proposed dimensional grouping (candidate fact vs. candidate dimensions) on the other, with a short note on why each table moved where it did.

slots.practicalActivity: For a retail sales process, draw the same Product dimension two ways: as a single flat star-schema dimension table, and as a normalized snowflake (Product -> Subcategory -> Category). Then write one sentence declaring the grain of the sales fact table (e.g., 'one row per product per order line') and explain why that specific grain statement rules out summarizing at the order level.
slots.deliverable: Two sketches of the Product dimension (star and snowflake form) plus a one-sentence grain declaration for the sales fact table with justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real business process you understand well (online course enrollments, gym check-ins, library loans, or a process from your own job). Identify the business process, declare its grain in one sentence, and list the dimensions that describe each occurrence (who, what, when, where). Sketch the resulting star schema on paper with the fact table in the center and each dimension as a satellite box.
slots.deliverable: A complete hand-drawn star schema diagram for a self-chosen business process: one fact table box with FK stubs, 4-6 dimension boxes, and a written grain statement.

slots.practicalActivity: Take five real business events (a retail sale, a bank's end-of-day account balance, an insurance claim moving through approval stages, a monthly subscription snapshot, and a student attending a class with no measurable value) and classify each as transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot, or factless. Write one sentence justifying each classification.
slots.deliverable: A 5-row table: business event | fact table type | one-sentence justification.

slots.practicalActivity: Design two fact tables on paper for an e-commerce business: (1) a transaction fact table at the order-line grain with columns for quantity, unit price, and discount; (2) a periodic snapshot fact table capturing daily inventory stock levels per warehouse per product. List the foreign keys and measures for each.
slots.deliverable: Two column lists (FKs + measures) — one for the order-line transaction fact, one for the daily inventory snapshot fact — each with a stated grain.

slots.practicalActivity: Design an accumulating snapshot fact table for an order fulfillment pipeline (order placed -> picked -> packed -> shipped -> delivered), with one date FK column per milestone that gets updated in place as the order progresses. Then design a factless fact table for tracking which students attended which class sessions (no measure, just the FKs for student, class, and date).
slots.deliverable: Two table layouts: the accumulating snapshot fact with 5 milestone date FKs and a note on which columns get updated vs. inserted-once, and the factless attendance fact with its FK list.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a Customer dimension table on paper: list 8-10 descriptive attributes (name, address, segment, loyalty tier, etc.), add a surrogate key column (customer_key, an integer with no business meaning), and keep the natural/business key (customer_id from the source system) as a separate attribute column.
slots.deliverable: A full column list for the Customer dimension showing the surrogate key, the natural key, and at least 8 descriptive attributes, with data types noted.

slots.practicalActivity: List three reasons a surrogate key beats a natural key for a Customer dimension that sources from two merging companies with overlapping customer IDs. Then look at a sales fact table design and identify which column (order number) is a degenerate dimension that lives directly on the fact table instead of in its own dimension table, and explain why it doesn't need one.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison (3 bullet points) of natural vs. surrogate keys for the merging-companies scenario, plus one sentence identifying and justifying the degenerate dimension on the sales fact table.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a conformed Date dimension and a conformed Product dimension that both a Sales fact table and an Inventory fact table can share. Specify the exact columns and keys so that a report can join both fact tables to the same Date dimension and get consistent calendar logic (fiscal periods, day-of-week) across both.
slots.deliverable: Column lists for the shared Date and Product dimensions, plus a one-paragraph explanation of what would break in cross-fact reporting if Sales and Inventory each built their own separate, non-conformed Date dimension.

slots.practicalActivity: For a Customer dimension, decide and justify the SCD handling for each of these attributes: date_of_birth (should never change), email_address (just overwrite), and signup_date (fixed at creation). Write out which ones are Type 0 and which are Type 1, and what happens to historical fact rows in each case.
slots.deliverable: A short table: attribute | SCD type (0 or 1) | one-sentence justification for each of the three attributes.

slots.practicalActivity: Fully design SCD Type 2 handling for a Customer dimension's mailing address. Write out the complete table structure: customer_key (surrogate, new row per change), customer_id (natural key, repeats across versions), address fields, effective_date, end_date, and is_current flag. Then walk through a concrete example: a customer moves from Dallas to Austin on 2024-06-01 — show the before row (with end_date and is_current updated) and the new row (with new surrogate key) exactly as they'd appear in the table.
slots.deliverable: The full Customer Type 2 table structure plus a worked before/after example showing both rows (old version closed out, new version inserted) with real sample values for the Dallas-to-Austin move.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a hybrid SCD pattern for an Employee dimension: use Type 3 (previous_region / current_region columns) for sales territory reassignment, and Type 2 (full row versioning) for salary band changes, on the same dimension table. Write out the complete column list showing both patterns coexisting.
slots.deliverable: A single Employee dimension column list showing the Type 3 previous/current region columns alongside the Type 2 effective_date/end_date/is_current versioning columns, with a short note on why salary history needed full versioning but territory didn't.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a staging table for a raw customer CSV feed arriving from a source system. Mirror the source columns as text/varchar types (no transformation yet), and add staging-specific columns: batch_id, load_timestamp, and source_filename. Explain in writing why staging keeps raw/untyped data instead of applying transformations immediately.
slots.deliverable: A staging table column list (mirrored source columns + batch_id + load_timestamp + source_filename) with a short paragraph on why the staging layer stays 'dumb' and untransformed.

slots.practicalActivity: For three source tables — a small, rarely-changing Country reference table (200 rows); a Customer table with occasional updates (500K rows); and a high-volume Orders table (50M rows, append-only) — decide and justify a full load vs. incremental load strategy for each, including what column (if any) you'd use to detect incremental changes.
slots.deliverable: A 3-row decision table: source table | full or incremental | justification | change-detection column (if incremental).

slots.practicalActivity: Write out 5 concrete data quality checks you would run against the staged Customer CSV from the earlier staging exercise (e.g., null checks on required fields, duplicate natural key detection, referential checks against known country codes, format checks on email/phone). Then add the audit/lineage columns (source_system, load_id, inserted_at, updated_at, row_hash) to the staging table design.
slots.deliverable: A list of 5 specific data quality checks for the Customer staging table, plus the final staging table column list with audit/lineage columns added.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a junk dimension that bundles 4-5 low-cardinality miscellaneous flags from an order (is_gift_wrapped, payment_method, is_rush_order, coupon_applied) into one combined dimension table with a single surrogate key. Then design the role-playing use of a single Date dimension against an Orders fact table that needs three separate date roles: order_date, ship_date, and delivery_date — show the three foreign keys and the view aliasing approach (order_date_dim, ship_date_dim, delivery_date_dim).
slots.deliverable: The junk dimension's column list with its combined surrogate key, plus a diagram showing one physical Date dimension joined three times (via three FKs/aliased views) to the Orders fact table.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a bridge table to resolve a many-to-many relationship: a Patient can have multiple Diagnoses, and a Diagnosis applies to multiple Patients, in a healthcare fact table context. Write out the bridge table structure (patient_key, diagnosis_key, and a weighting factor column if allocating a measure like cost across diagnoses) and show how it sits between the Patient dimension, Diagnosis dimension, and the fact table.
slots.deliverable: A bridge table column list plus a short diagram showing how the fact table joins to Patient and Diagnosis through the bridge, including the weighting-factor approach for allocating a shared cost measure.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the late-arriving-dimension handling procedure for a sale that arrives in the fact table before its matching new Customer row exists in the dimension (inferred/placeholder member row, later updated in place). Then design an aggregate table that pre-summarizes the daily Sales fact table up to monthly-by-region totals, and explain which queries would hit the aggregate instead of the base fact table.
slots.deliverable: A written procedure (numbered steps) for handling a late-arriving Customer dimension row, plus the column list for a monthly-by-region Sales aggregate table with a note on the query pattern it serves.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the Sales star schema designed earlier (fact + Customer, Product, Date dimensions) and write the physical design decisions: which schema/database the fact and dimension tables live in, data types and nullability for each FK and measure column, and an indexing plan (clustered index on the fact table's date key for range scans, nonclustered indexes on each other FK, and indexes on each dimension's surrogate key).
slots.deliverable: A physical design document: table-by-table column definitions with data types, plus an indexing plan listing which columns get which index type and why.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a partitioning strategy for a Sales fact table that holds 5 years of daily transactions (hundreds of millions of rows). Choose the partition key (date), the partition interval (monthly), write out the first 6 partition boundary values, and explain how this speeds up queries that filter to a recent date range and how it simplifies purging old data.
slots.deliverable: A partition scheme specification: partition key, interval, the first 6 boundary dates, and a short explanation of the query-performance and data-lifecycle benefits.

slots.practicalActivity: Apply a consistent naming convention (fact_ / dim_ prefixes, _key suffix for surrogate keys, _id suffix for natural keys, snake_case) across every table and column from the Sales star schema designed in earlier hours, renaming anything that doesn't conform. Then write a one-page data dictionary entry for the fact table and one dimension, documenting each column's meaning, type, and source.
slots.deliverable: A renamed, convention-compliant column list for the full Sales star schema, plus a one-page data dictionary excerpt (fact table + one dimension) with column descriptions.

slots.practicalActivity: Choose a real business process to model end-to-end for the capstone (e.g., a retail store's order fulfillment, a clinic's patient visits, a SaaS company's subscription billing, or a process from your own job). Write a one-page project brief: the business process, its grain, the key business questions it must answer, and the source data you're assuming is available.
slots.deliverable: A one-page capstone project brief naming the chosen business process, its grain, 3-5 business questions it must answer, and the assumed source tables/feeds.

lessons.title: Capstone: Modeling a Real Business Process

slots.practicalActivity: Using the project brief from the kickoff hour, fully model the chosen business process: draw the complete star schema (fact table with correct grain and fact type, all dimension tables with surrogate keys), decide the SCD type for every dimension attribute that can change, and note any advanced patterns needed (junk dimension, role-playing dates, bridge table, or aggregate table).
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone dimensional model diagram: fact table (with declared grain and type), every dimension table with SCD-type decisions annotated per attribute, and any advanced patterns called out.

slots.practicalActivity: Translate the capstone dimensional model into an actual physical schema: write CREATE TABLE statements (in SQL, on paper or in a script file) for the fact table and every dimension, including surrogate keys, natural keys, SCD Type 2 versioning columns where needed, foreign key constraints, and the naming conventions and indexing plan established earlier in the course.
slots.deliverable: A complete set of CREATE TABLE statements for the capstone's fact and dimension tables, with keys, SCD columns, constraints, and indexes all specified.

slots.practicalActivity: Assemble the capstone into a portfolio piece: combine the project brief, the star schema diagram, the SCD decisions, and the physical CREATE TABLE statements into a single document or slide deck. Write a short narrative explaining the key design trade-offs you made (grain choice, which SCD types you picked and why, any bridge/junk/role-playing patterns used) as if presenting to a hiring manager.
slots.deliverable: A polished capstone portfolio document/deck (brief + diagram + SCD decisions + physical schema + trade-off narrative) ready to show in a job interview or portfolio site.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can take a real business process and design a production-ready dimensional warehouse for it from scratch: choosing the correct grain and fact table type, building properly keyed dimension tables with the right slowly changing dimension strategy per attribute, designing a staging layer with data quality and audit controls, applying advanced patterns like bridge and junk dimensions, and delivering an indexed, partitioned, documented physical schema.
